title: Continued Sports Activity, Using a Pain-Monitoring Model, during Rehabilitation in Patients with Achilles Tendinopathy
authors: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J
journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
population: 38 patients with Achilles tendinopathy, randomly allocated to two groups of 19
findings: Thirty-eight patients with Achilles tendinopathy were randomly allocated to two groups. The exercise training group (n = 19) was allowed, with the use of a pain-monitoring model, to continue Achilles tendon-loading activity such as running and jumping, whereas the active rest group (n = 19) had to stop such activities during the first 6 weeks (abstract).

All patients were rehabilitated according to an identical rehabilitation program; the primary outcomes were the Swedish version of the VISA-A questionnaire (VISA-A-S) and pain level during tendon-loading activity (abstract).

No significant differences in the rate of improvement were found between the groups; both improved significantly (P < .01) against baseline at all evaluations. Mean (SD) VISA-A-S was 57 (15.8) at baseline and 85 (12.7) at 12 months in the exercise group, and 57 (15.7) and 91 (8.2) in the active rest group (abstract).

The authors conclude that no negative effects could be demonstrated from continuing tendon-loading activity such as running and jumping with the use of a pain-monitoring model during treatment, and that pain-monitored, tendon-loading activity might be a valuable option (abstract).
limitations: Abstract only: the full text is closed access and was not read, so the pain thresholds of the model are not quoted from this paper. The 5 of 10 limit and the rule that pain settles by the next morning, which the 2026-11-12 review attributed to it, are not in its abstract; a systematic review (smith-2017-painful-exercise-meta) prints those two criteria for the same group's 2001 trial, not for this one. Small trial (19 per group) in patients with a diagnosed Achilles tendinopathy under supervised treatment, not in healthy runners and not for pain in other places. Non-inferiority was not tested: no difference in 38 people does not show equivalence.
implications: Supports a statement that, in one supervised Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation, continuing running and jumping under a pain-monitoring model did not do worse over 12 months than 6 weeks of stopping them.

Gives no threshold for the engine: the numbers of the model are not in the abstract, the population is under treatment, and the trial says nothing about a runner who is not being treated or about any site but the Achilles tendon.
